nodes.question: What role do socioeconomic inequalities play in environmental sustainability efforts?
nodes.answer: Socioeconomic inequalities hinder cooperation in sustainability efforts and contribute to biodiversity loss.
nodes.paragraph: As the global com- munity faces escalating challenges such as climate change, resource depletion, and bio- diversity loss, the need for practical, scalable, and equitable environmental protection strategies has become critical. International efforts, such as the World Bank S Global Program on Sustainability (GPS), underscore the importance of integrating environmen- tal considerations into public and private sector decision-making (GPS, 2019). However, rapid economic growth often exacerbates environmental degradation through resource Extended author information available on the last page of the article H. M. U. D. Qadri et al. over-exploitation and pollution from energy-intensive industries (Hamaguchi, 2024; Xiao et al., 2012). Socioeconomic inequalities further amplify these challenges, hindering coop- eration in sustainability efforts and contributing to biodiversity loss (Baland et al., 2018; Mikkelson et al., 2007). A growing body of research highlights the crucial role of socioeconomic factors such as income, education, and employment stability in shaping environmental attitudes and behaviors, with distinct patterns emerging between higher and lower socioeconomic groups. Higher socioeconomic groups, characterized by greater financial stability and envi- ronmental awareness, are more likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviors, including energy-saving measures and sustainable consumption practices (Du et al., 2024; Ivkovi & Mandi , 2024; Meyer, 2016).

nodes.question: In what area has the application of social ecology theory been primarily limited in Botswana, according to the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The application of social ecology theory has primarily been limited to wildlife management in Botswana.
nodes.paragraph: 2013, p. 7 of 20; Blanco 2011; Budiharta et al. 2016; Ostrom 2009). All these studies suggest that local communities involvement is crucial in the sustainable management of resources. Social ecology theory has also been used in waste management studies and local knowledge in sub-Saharan Africa (Muheirwe et al. 2023, p. 1; Anokye & Mohammed 2024). Both studies highlight the importance of local knowl- edge to sustainable waste management strategies and criti- cize the apparent disregard for local knowledge as a viable alternative solution. On the other hand studies on Botswana communities using the social ecology theory have been limited to wildlife management (Blackie and Sowa 2019 ; Mbaiwa 2015; Mbaiwa and Hambira 2023). While the social ecology theory has been successfully applied to wildlife management and Community-Based Natural Resource Management (CBNRM) in Botswana, the use of the SES framework in waste management studies is still rare. Despite government efforts to regulate waste management through legislation, many households continue to use harmful practices like burning, burying, or dumping waste. To address these gaps, this study aims to explore the role of local knowledge as a solution for enhancing waste management in Borakalalo ward in Molepolole, Botswana.
